pitch_detail.notes: From the ~6,900 ft Clark-Johnson col, drop about 100 ft and climb Johnson's lower snowfield to its upper-left corner. From there a narrow ledge traverses left (south), squeezing past an outcrop onto the upper snowfield. The ledge is easy but narrows to a few feet over a gravelly outsloping drop to upper Surprise Basin; it is easier than the ramps that lead straight up.

Cross the upper snowfield to a little left of its centre and exit onto a rubbly, low-angle gully. Follow it up, then back right along the base of a low wall that leads around behind Sweat Spire and Gasp Pinnacle to the summit block. The trap is leaving the snowfield too far right: the gullies under the spires steepen into rounded steps that are hard to reverse. Late season this is all loose scree and rock.

The summit block is split by several chimneys; take the rightmost, the only reasonable one. It is steep but secure when tucked inside, finishing by stemming with back on one wall and feet on the other; a short walk up the crest then reaches the top. The east face below is very loose, so descending parties should face in and test every hold. A short 5th-class variation climbs the notch between Gasp and Sweat instead.

review.changed: Rewrote all 3 rows (labels kept). The stored rows described a traverse around the south, then east, then north side of the summit block; the researched line is lower snowfield, leftward ledge, upper snowfield, rubbly gully behind the spires, then the rightmost chimney. Added lengthM 15 only on the chimney (a 50 ft chimney is stated for this route). The sequence rests mainly on one detailed trip report, corroborated in outline by a second report and the guidebook route list, so capped at medium. No crux flag (no source calls one section the crux).
review.other_findings: beta says the route keeps to class 3 'by skirting right of Gasp Pinnacle'; both trip reports go LEFT of / behind the Sweat-Gasp spires (the notch between them is the separate 5th-class variant). descent_text's optional 30-50 ft rappel below the summit block is not supported by any source read (parties downclimbed the chimney and east face) - not contradicted either.

pitch_detail.notes: From Lower Snowy Lake make a slightly rising traverse toward the west face, crossing talus and scree below minor cliffs and through some scrub to the main talus slope under the face. The talus traverse is short but strenuous; a large reddish boulder partway across is a useful aim point.

A headwall blocks direct entry to the main gully. Climb talus and scree up its left (west) side to the start of a ledge system that crosses above the headwall to the mouth of a large cave (about 20 ft high, visible from the lakes). The ledge looks worse from below than it is. Beyond the cave it reaches the entrance to the main gully; helmets on from here.

Keep to the right side of the gully, which has the most ledges and cairns; the middle and left are steeper, more exposed, and the whitish centre has few holds. Zigzag up right-side ledges, briefly leaving the gully where needed, for about 150 ft to a small promontory in the centre, then follow a ledge system far right and back to centre. Surface rubble is everywhere - move one at a time in constrictions.

Climb the centre of the brown gully, a narrower mini-gully of darker rock inside the main one; the options either side are more technical. Where the gully narrows the climbing is a short, smooth slab. The route stays near the top of class 3 here, and any rock knocked loose funnels straight onto parties below.

Continue to the very base of the distinct white V in the white headwall at the gully's head, then go through a small notch up and right out of the gully. Do not start up the ledges too soon - several end in technical ground. Traverse south on ledges, following cairns, looking for the easiest place to gain the south ridge; this is where parties most often go off route.

Once on the south ridge crest, class 3 over blocks with one exposed move leads to the summit and its famous cairn, roughly 7 ft tall and reportedly built by the 1913 first-ascent party. Descend the same way, keeping to the cairned ledges on the right side of the gully (as seen facing uphill) rather than its steep centre.

review.changed: 6 rows kept, notes rewritten from the detailed standard-route description (cave ledge, right-side gully ledges, promontory, brown gully, white V, notch, traverse to south ridge). Renamed 'Crux slab' to 'Brown gully slab': it is the same ground, but no source calls it the crux, and the stored '~15 ft of class 4, often wet' and 'Class 4 (to ~5.4)' grade have no source - one description says a smooth slab where the gully narrows, and the main description says the route never exceeds class 3 though it comes close. Crux flag, lengths and the wet-rock claim left out.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 'Class 3-4': the standard-route description rates it class 3 ('should never exceed class 3'); the 5.6 'SW Gully Upper South Ridge' is a different line. beta's 'second gully containing roughly 15 ft of slabby class 4 (sometimes wet)' is unsourced. Two published descriptions differ on how the gully is entered (cave ledge vs. a notch in the west ridge and a gully marked by a gendarme); the table follows the cave-ledge version, which the approach column and three trip reports also describe.

pitch_detail.pitch: 1: Easy Pass Trailhead to Easy Pass
pitch_detail.notes: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on Hwy 20 the trail climbs about 2,800 ft in roughly 3.6 miles to the 6,540 ft pass. The upper trail crosses avalanche paths and can be lost under snow into early summer, when the final slopes below the pass are a snow climb (axe useful). Logan is visible far to the southwest from the pass.

pitch_detail.pitch: 2: Easy Pass to Fisher Creek valley
pitch_detail.notes: Descend the steep switchbacking trail into the Fisher Creek valley and follow it down-valley to where the side valley draining the Douglas Glacier comes in from the south, about 4 miles from the pass at roughly 3,900 ft. Note that the switchbacks must be regained on the way out. Fisher Camp and Cosho Camp are along this trail.

pitch_detail.pitch: 3: Fisher Creek to Douglas Creek (off-trail bushwhack)
pitch_detail.notes: Cross Fisher Creek on logs and stay on the east (left) side of Douglas Creek. The first mile is flat open forest with bogs. The lower basin (~4,000 ft) is an old avalanche zone now choked with head-high slide alder and hidden stream channels - progress can drop to a crawl. Aim for the rounded wooded knob at its head (Point 4805) and pass it up and right to the upper basin (~4,700 ft), where camps sit along the east side. Snow cover makes this far easier.

Climb the upper-basin headwall by its weakest line, on the west side a little north of where the glacier hangs down, among waterfalls and brush holds; off-line it becomes class 4. Above the steepest part, traverse level left (south) at about 5,800 ft around a small rock buttress and tree band to the glacier toe. A longer detour around the left side avoids the headwall and may be easier in descent; parties unsure of their line may need a rappel.

Rope up and climb about 2,200 vertical ft to the upper bowl, turning right near 8,000 ft and following the narrowing glacier to the obvious notch (~8,550 ft) at its northern head. Crevasses are real but mostly end-runnable; where the glacier narrows near 8,000 ft a crevasse can span almost its full width, and staying to one side (usually right) avoids the broken centre. Late season the toe melts back to bare slab.

From the notch, leave the snow swale by circling right or climbing its steep (40-50°) bank, then continue on snow or loose talus through a chute to another open slope. Near the crest, scramble rightward onto it a little south of the summit and follow the airy ridge, with more exposure on the west. A false summit comes first; downclimb from it to reach the true top. A short rappel may be needed coming off the summit ridge.

review.changed: 6 rows kept with their labels (the stored table already treats the approach as sections). Removed the stored 'AI2 / steep ice' claim and the 'traverse to meet Banded Glacier' idea - no source supports either; the route climbs the Douglas to the notch at its head. Replaced '1.5 miles, 1,500 ft loss' for row 2 with the ~4 miles to the Douglas Creek junction the route description gives, and dropped row 6's '~300 vertical feet' (notch ~8,550 ft vs summit 9,087 ft is ~540 ft). No lengthM (no pitch lengths exist for this glacier route). Rows 1-3 rest on two sources, rows 4-6 mostly on one detailed route description plus one trip report, hence medium.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 'Grade II, Class 4': the route description rates it Grade III, class 3 rock (a trip report calls the summit 3rd/4th class) - worth a look. beta says the route 'traverses to meet Banded Glacier' before the summit block: the Douglas route tops out at the ~8,550 ft notch at the Douglas Glacier's head (the Douglas/Banded col) and then climbs rock - there is no Banded Glacier traverse. descent_text offers 'Descend the Banded Glacier via the Banded-Douglas col to reach the Fisher Creek basin' as a routine alternative; not researched, but the Banded is described as badly broken (crevasse band spanning most of its width), so presenting it as a casual descent option deserves checking. rappels=1 is consistent (a minor summit-ridge rappel is mentioned as possible).

pitch_detail.notes: The boot path leaves the old Middle Fork road opposite a large broken log, about half a mile short of the road's end. It climbs through brush and a cairned boulder field; the half-mile below the lower lake is faint. From the lower lake a path climbs east to the upper lake - stay near the inlet stream (north side of the upper lake's outlet), since straying left runs into cliff bands.

From the upper lake climb the gully to Hardscrabble Gap, the obvious ~5,750 ft pass in the ridge. Into early summer it is a snow couloir; once the snow line retreats, the lower few hundred feet mean picking a way around cliff bands and over talus. An axe is useful on firm morning snow and for controlling a glissade on the way down.

pitch_detail.pitch: North slope slab to east ridge
pitch_detail.notes: From the gap drop onto the glacier-polished granite slabs of the north slope, dotted with tarns and snow patches that linger late, then follow the long east (northeast) ridge to the 6,680 ft summit. It is never steep but it is a long grind; early season the final stretch can be steep snow on the west side of the crest. There are bivy spots on top and sometimes meltwater just below it.

review.changed: 3 rows kept with their labels, notes expanded: the big-log start point, the cairned boulder field and the faint section below the lower lake, the cliff-band trap left of the inlet, the gap's elevation (~5,750 ft), the snow couloir and the cliff-and-talus stretch when the snow is gone, and the final ridge grind. No lengthM, crux or grades beyond class 2 (none are stated for sections).
review.other_findings: grade is null; every source rates this route class 2 (the upper gully to the gap is snow early season). The same ridge is called the 'east ridge' in one source and the 'northeast shoulder' in another - same ground.

pitch_detail.pitch: Highway turnout (~1,900 ft) to NW ridge crest
pitch_detail.notes: From the turnout opposite the large boulder field, climb straight up the steep timbered hillside just left (east) of the boulder field for about 450 ft, then angle left for about 200 ft more to gain the northwest ridgeline. It is relentlessly steep from the first step, on a faint path at best.

Follow the forested ridge straight up. Several cliff bands cross it; in snow season they are turned by snow ramps. Snowshoes usually go on around 4,000 ft, though one cliffy section just above may need them off again. Around 5,400 ft the trees open and the upper route and summit come into view.

pitch_detail.pitch: ~5,400 ft over Point 6315' to summit ridge (~7,100 ft)
pitch_detail.notes: Head southeast up the open ridge over Point 6315'. The last several hundred feet to the summit ridge are steep, with cornices along the crest overhanging the north face - stay well back from the edge, keeping to the trees while they last. A breakable wind crust over powder can make this slow going. Small glaciers lie on the north side of the summit ridge.

pitch_detail.pitch: Summit ridge to true summit (7,408 ft)
pitch_detail.notes: The final roughly 300 ft to the true summit is a scramble over exposed mixed rock and snow. Where the crest is corniced or steep, moving off it onto the back side, away from the cornices, avoids the worst of it. The top holds an antenna/repeater station, which must not be entered or tampered with.

review.changed: 4 rows kept. Relabelled row 2 ('NW Ridge over Point 6315' to ~5,400 ft') and row 3 because Point 6315' lies ABOVE 5,400 ft, so it belonged in row 3; row 4's summit height changed from 7,426 to 7,408 ft (the elevation given for the true summit). Row 4 grade changed from 'Class 3 scramble' to a terrain chip - sources say 'scrambling' over exposed mixed rock and snow but give no class. Added the cornice hazard, the snowshoe/cliff-band detail and the summit repeater. No lengthM or crux.
sources_consulted: https://cnmtstuartclimbproject.blogspot.com/2017/04/route-ruby-mountain-nw-ridge-route.html (quotes a trip report and the route directions)
https://besthikesbc.ca/hiking-ruby-mountain-in-the-north-cascades/ (Happy Creek variant - used only for context, not for this table)
review.other_findings: The label '(7,426 ft)' disagreed with the 7,408 ft summit elevation the route sources give; the area row's elevation may want checking. Note that the other popular snow-season line (Happy Creek from Ross Dam, with its boulder field at ~3,500-3,600 ft) is a different route; its beta should not be merged into this row.

pitch_detail.pitch: Sol Duc TH to Heart Lake
pitch_detail.notes: From the Sol Duc road-end trailhead (~2,000 ft) pass Sol Duc Falls and the Deer Lake junction (about 1 mile) and climb about 6 more miles up the Sol Duc valley to Heart Lake (4,800 ft). The lake has several good camps; a wilderness permit and bear canister are required, and permits here are in heavy demand.

Climb about 1.5 miles to the High Divide crest (~5,100 ft) and follow it toward Cat Basin, about 3 miles, to where the maintained trail ends. A thin, worn path continues along the ridge below Cat Peak through trees and brush to the start of the Catwalk. Late in the season water up here is limited to snowbanks and sinkholes, so carry enough.

A narrow rock and heather ridgetop links Cat Peak to the Bailey Range: high class 2 to low class 3 moves with serious exposure, where a fall could be fatal. Before mid-July lingering snow can make it much harder. Past it, push through brush to Boston Charlie's Camp, a small, sloping, exposed site with a brackish sinkhole pond; filter the water, and treat it as an emergency bivy rather than a planned camp.

A semi-cairned path switchbacks up Carrie's southwest ridge, about 2,000 ft in under a mile; grassy at first, then grass and rock outcrops as it narrows. Near 6,500 ft it contours around the top of a big south-facing scree basin ringed with summits; the rock is loose, so helmets on. The true summit is at the far right (east) side of the basin, reached via the summit ridge. Early season, snow in the basin calls for an axe.

review.changed: 4 rows kept with their labels. Removed row 2's 'no water beyond Heart Lake' (there is a brackish pond at Boston Charlie's, plus snowbanks and sinkholes on the High Divide). Added the maintained-trail end, the brush and emergency-only nature of Boston Charlie's Camp, the snow-before-mid-July note on the Catwalk, and the basin contour, loose rock and summit location on the final row. No lengthM or crux.

classification.name: Proposed name: 'Southwest Ridge via High Divide and the Catwalk' (do not apply without review). Evidence: (1) the SummitPost route says to climb from Boston Charlie's Camp and 'gain the southwest ridge of Mt. Carrie', grassy then rocky, to a scree basin with the summit at its far right; (2) the Outdoor Project guide is titled 'Southwest Rib route via High Divide + Bogachiel' and follows 'the southwest ridge of Mount Carrie' from Boston Charlie's to ~6,500 ft; (3) the Olympic climbing guide lists Carrie's only route as 'Route 1, Grade I, Class 2 via the High Divide Trail and Cat Walk'. Geometry agrees: the Catwalk runs northeast from Cat Peak, so it delivers climbers to Carrie's southwest side. No source describes a southeast route, and no route runs from Hurricane Ridge (which is only a viewpoint of Carrie's north side). 'Southwest Rib' is an acceptable alternative wording; 'Route 1 / High Divide and Catwalk' is the guidebook's name.

review.other_findings: Name 'Southeast Route via Hurricane Ridge / Cat Basin' is wrong on both counts (see classification.name); the overview and approach already say so in prose. Summit elevation differs between sources (6,995 ft vs 7,156 ft) - not researched further. The route row's own discipline/grade ('scrambling', 'Class 2-3 with steep snow early season') match the sources.
